title: Blast Hits Riyadh Airport, Trump Says U.S. May Join Saudi Strikes on Houthis
snippet: Multiple injuries were reported at Riyadh's main airport following a strike on Saturday, prompting President Trump to consider military action against Houthi forces.
content:
RIYADH — A strike hit King Khalid International Airport in Saudi Arabia's capital on Saturday, leaving several people injured and grounding flights across the region as tensions escalate between the kingdom and Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels.

Eyewitnesses reported seeing a flash in the sky before an explosion rocked a departure gate area, causing a section of the ceiling to collapse. Dozens of ambulances rushed to the facility as Saudi civil aviation authorities suspended all airport operations. Flight-tracking data showed incoming flights diverted or canceled as air traffic over the capital ground to a halt.

Trump Weighs Direct U.S. Involvement

The attack immediately drew a reaction from Washington. Speaking to reporters outside the White House, President Donald Trump signaled that the United States could step in to back Saudi counter-strikes against the Houthis.

"We may. We're going to look at it," Trump said when asked about potential U.S. participation in military operations. "We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision. We move very quickly."

Following the blast, the U.S. Embassy in Riyadh issued a security advisory strongly urging American citizens to avoid the airport and surrounding areas. Foreign embassies from Canada, the United Kingdom, and Ireland also acknowledged ongoing military activity impacting the facility.

Security Defenses Questioned Ahead of Major Summits

Saturday's incident marks the third time this week that Riyadh's primary airport has come under fire. Previous strikes left four people dead and exposed critical vulnerabilities in the kingdom's air defense capabilities, with officials acknowledging that early warning systems failed to sound an alarm prior to Saturday's explosion.

The Houthis have declared Saudi airspace a military zone following a recent Saudi-backed offensive in Yemen. Several major international airlines, including Etihad, Qatar Airways, and Kuwait Airways, have canceled flights into the Saudi capital.

The security crisis comes at a critical moment for Riyadh, which is scheduled to host major international investment and energy summits in the coming days. Conference organizers stated Saturday that the events will proceed as planned with heightened security measures in place.
